messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Potter
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Vignette:
Amin Hossain was a 75-year-old South Asian man who had lived for many years with his wife in the United States, working as a potter and taking quiet pride in the steady, practical rhythm of his craft. In conversation he was reserved but attentive, and he spoke of his work with a kind of worn affection, as something that had once defined him. That sense of himself had been shaken back in the years when he and his family fled as refugees. He did not tell the event as a single, orderly story. Instead, when he tried, it came out in broken fragments: the sound of cars coming too close, men shouting, the sight of police in uniform, the feeling that everything had turned at once and he needed to move, though he could not later say exactly how the danger unfolded. He said that when he tries to put it into words, the experience seems to resist language, as if the most frightening parts were only ever registered as flashes. What remained were pieces that do not fit together cleanly, but that return to him with an intensity that makes ordinary memories seem pale by comparison. He described them as more real than the things happening around him now, as if the scene were still close enough to touch.

Over time, certain places and moments began to feel loaded with that same danger. Funerals and cemeteries were especially difficult for him, not because he was unable to understand grief, but because the atmosphere of graves and mourning brought back the unmistakable closeness of death from the time he fled. Even a grief-related event could leave him tense and watchful, wanting to get away before anything in the air changed. The same was true when he heard cars approaching suddenly, especially in a street or parking lot where the sound seemed to come up behind him. In those moments he would stop and look around, his attention narrowing to the possible direction of threat. The presence of police was similarly activating. A uniform at a distance was enough to pull his body into alertness, and he became careful about where he stood, how he moved, and whether he was being noticed. He had come to believe that he had to be especially careful because one never knew what could happen next, and that sense of uncertainty was never far from him.

Amin’s efforts to manage this state had become part of his daily life. He was constantly scanning his surroundings for signs that something might go wrong, even in ordinary settings. In the workshop where he made pottery, his gaze would drift from the wheel to the door, to the street outside, to any approaching vehicle he could hear. In the neighborhood, a passing car could interrupt his focus and send him checking who was near, where they were standing, and whether there was any reason to leave. He also found himself avoiding any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation. If there was tension with a shop owner, a neighbor, or even a family discussion that seemed likely to turn sharp, he tended to withdraw or change the subject. He preferred not to risk an argument, and he often explained this in plain terms: he could not deal with even the slightest upset. At times this had narrowed his life more than he liked to admit. He and his wife had once attended community gatherings more freely, but over time he began to decline invitations, especially those that might become emotionally charged or celebratory in ways that felt exposing. He avoided positive events too, including situations that might make him feel hopeful or happy, because he found that such feelings left him vulnerable to disappointment and made him uneasy about what might follow.

He spoke with some shame about how little like himself he sometimes felt now. The work of the potter had once given shape to his days and a sense of competence, but he had come to believe that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him. On difficult days he would look at the clay and feel that the steadiness, concentration, and confidence he used to rely on were no longer there in the same way. This was painful not only because of the work itself, but because it touched his identity as a husband, craftsman, and elder in his family. His wife had noticed that he was quieter and more guarded, and while she remained supportive, their world had gradually become smaller and more careful.

By the time he sought help, Amin was doing so because the pattern had become hard to live with. The funerals he could not attend, the roads he crossed warily, the police he tried not to see, and the constant checking of his surroundings had left him exhausted and increasingly isolated. He wanted to understand why these moments still struck him with such force and why the memories came back in pieces that felt so vivid and immediate. More than anything, he hoped for relief from the sense that danger could appear at any moment and that he would not be able to meet it.
